summary: EDNS(0) lets a DNS receiver signal how large a UDP message it accepts, enabling large responses, but large UDP messages are more likely to be fragmented, and IP fragmentation has exposed weaknesses. This informational document describes ways to avoid fragmentation in DNS over UDP.

plainLanguage.summary: Big packages get chopped into pieces that can be lost or tampered with. This gives tips for keeping DNS answers small enough to travel whole.

questions: how to avoid ip fragmentation in dns
what is the recommended edns udp payload size
subtitle: Practical rules for keeping DNS answers small enough that UDP never has to split them into IP fragments.

tldr.problem: EDNS(0) lets DNS servers send large UDP responses, but large UDP messages are more likely to be fragmented, and fragmented DNS responses expose requestors to off-path cache poisoning.
tldr.mechanism: Responders and requestors keep UDP payloads within the smaller of the interface MTU, the configured network MTU and a recommended 1400 bytes. Requestors drop fragments, and operators publish smaller responses so that TCP is used when a response will not fit.
tldr.outcome: The document is Informational, not a Best Current Practice, because some recommendations lack real-world experience with operating system and socket option limits. It anticipates a later BCP.

today: RFC 9715 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It was published as Informational rather than a Best Current Practice, and the authors expect to publish an updated document as a BCP once operating systems and implementations give more experience with the recommendations.

sections.title: Why Fragmentation Is a Problem for DNS
sections.content:
The EDNS(0) mechanism from RFC 6891 lets a DNS receiver announce how large a UDP message it can take. That makes big UDP responses possible, but a UDP packet larger than the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of some network on its path invites IP fragmentation.

The RFC says fragmented DNS UDP responses have systemic weaknesses that expose the requestor to DNS cache poisoning from off-path attackers. It points to RFC 8900, which states that IP fragmentation introduces fragility to Internet communication.

TCP can pick segment sizes that fit the path. DNS over UDP has little datagram size elasticity and no insight into IP header and option size, so it has to make more conservative estimates. The document is primarily meant for DNS use on the global Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Big messages can get chopped up on the way, and the chopped pieces are easy to tamper with. DNS should try to send messages that never need chopping.

sections.title: Recommendations for Responders and Requestors
sections.content:
Section 3 lists numbered recommendations, R1 to R7, for nodes with global IP addresses. Private and local networks are out of scope.

For UDP responders: should not use IPv6 fragmentation (R1); should configure systems to prevent fragmentation when sending replies, where that can be done safely (R2); and should compose responses that fit in the minimum of the requestor's offered maximum UDP payload size, the interface MTU, the network MTU configured by operators, and the recommended maximum DNS/UDP payload size of 1400 (R3). If the responder sees an immediate error that the packet exceeds the path MTU, it may rebuild the response to fit or with the TC bit set (R4).

For UDP requestors: limit the requestor's maximum UDP payload size to the same kind of minimum, with 1400 as the recommended ceiling and smaller values allowed (R5); drop fragmented DNS/UDP responses without IP reassembly, at the firewall function, to avoid cache poisoning (R6); and, because responses may be dropped, eventually try alternative transport protocols (R7).

On the mechanism for R2, BSD-like systems can use the IP Don't Fragment (DF) flag, while Linux needs the IP_MTU_DISCOVER socket option. The RFC notes that enabling IPv4 Path MTU Discovery for UDP in current Linux versions is considered harmful and dangerous.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers should pack answers in boxes no bigger than the smallest door on the way. Askers should throw away any answer that arrives in pieces and ask again using a sturdier method.

sections.title: What DNS Operators Can Do
sections.content:
Large responses usually come from zone configuration, so people who publish DNS data should aim for small responses. Four recommendations follow:

  • R8: use a smaller number of name servers.
  • R9: use a smaller number of A/AAAA records for a domain name.
  • R10: use a minimal-responses configuration, which keeps only mandatory and required data in a response.
  • R11: use a DNSSEC algorithm with smaller signatures and keys. ECDSA and EdDSA signatures are smaller than RSA signatures of equivalent cryptographic strength.

The RFC admits it is hard to set a specific upper limit for R8, R9 and R11. It is enough that every response from the DNS servers stays below the size set by R3 and R5.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want your parcel to fit in the mailbox, send fewer things and wrap them tightly. Servers can list fewer names, leave out extras and use shorter secret signatures.

sections.title: Non-Compliant Servers
sections.content:
Some authoritative servers deviate from the DNS standard. Some ignore the EDNS(0) requestor's maximum UDP payload size and return large UDP responses, and some do not support TCP at all.

The RFC's position is that such behavior cannot become an implementation or configuration constraint for the rest of the DNS. If failure results, it must be localized to the non-compliant servers.
sections.plainLanguage: If one shop ignores the rules, everyone else should not have to change for it. Only that shop should suffer the problems.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A DNS receiver cannot trust fragmented UDP datagrams, mainly because UDP port numbers and DNS message identifiers are each only 16 bits, and both are likely to sit in the first fragment. Earlier research cited in the RFC shows effective off-path cache poisoning with IP fragmentation, and that off-path attackers can interfere with Path MTU Discovery to make authoritative servers produce fragmented responses.

DNSSEC is a countermeasure, but delegation responses are not signed, so an injected delegation can still cause denial of service. Avoiding poisoning avoids those validation failures.

Avoiding fragmentation has a cost: a requestor behind a small MTU network may see UDP timeouts and fall back to TCP, which suggests it was relying on fragmentation before. For resolver operators, the RFC advises implementing R5 and R6: configure the firewall to discard incoming DNS response packets with a non-zero Fragment Offset or a More Fragments flag of 1 on IPv4, and packets with IPv6 Fragment Headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Pieces of a chopped-up message are easy to swap for fake ones, because the secret check numbers are short. So the safest thing is to refuse messages that arrive in pieces.

items.label: No IPv6 fragmentation
items.desc: UDP responders should not use IPv6 fragmentation.

items.label: Prevent fragmentation
items.desc: Responders configure systems to prevent fragmenting replies, where safe.

items.label: Fit responses
items.desc: Responses fit the minimum of requestor size, interface MTU, configured MTU and 1400.

items.label: React to size errors
items.desc: On an immediate size error, rebuild the response to fit or set the TC bit.

items.label: Limit requestor size
items.desc: Requestors limit their maximum UDP payload size, with 1400 as the recommended maximum.

items.label: Drop fragments
items.desc: Requestors drop fragmented DNS/UDP responses without reassembly.

items.label: Try other transport
items.desc: Requestors eventually try alternative transport protocols.
